parts.label: (a)(i)

markscheme_points.text: energy required to separate nucleons (of a nucleus)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what holds protons and neutrons together inside a nucleus, and what you would have to do to pull them completely apart from each other.
Hint 2: For a full definition, state that the separation must be complete - the nucleons end up isolated with no nuclear attraction left between them.
parts.proper_answer: The energy required to separate all the nucleons in a nucleus to infinite separation from each other.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture what binding means**
Think of the nucleus as tightly glued together by the strong nuclear force. Protons and neutrons - collectively called nucleons - are not just sitting together, they are bound. To unbind them you must do work on them.

Step 2: **Build the full definition**
So binding energy is the minimum energy you must supply to break that glue and separate every nucleon from every other one. To be complete you must separate them to infinity, where there is no attractive force left. That is: energy required to separate all nucleons to infinite separation.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a nuclear fission reaction.

markscheme_points.text: a (single) large nucleus divides to form (smaller nuclei)

hints: Hint 1: Start from the word fission meaning splitting - think whether you start with one nucleus or many, and whether that starting nucleus is light or heavy.
Hint 2: Describe what is produced - how many smaller nuclei form from that one parent nucleus.
parts.proper_answer: A single heavy (large) nucleus splits (divides) to form two smaller nuclei of similar size, with release of neutrons and energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start with one heavy nucleus**
Fission is not joining things together and it is not radioactive decay giving out an alpha particle. You begin with one single large, heavy, unstable nucleus such as uranium-235.

Step 2: **Split into smaller nuclei**
That parent nucleus divides into two (usually) smaller daughter nuclei of roughly comparable size, plus a few neutrons. The total binding energy increases, so energy is released in the process.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: A student suggests that one possible nuclear reaction is $$^{56}_{26}\text{Fe} + ^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow ^{20}_{9}\text{F} + ^{37}_{17}\text{Cl}$$ The binding energy per nucleon of a nucleus varies with the nucleon number. Use this variation to explain why the reaction would not result in an overall release of energy.

markscheme_points.guidance: award 1 mark for any one of the following

markscheme_points.text: resulting nuclei are of similar size
combined mass of smaller nuclei is less
binding energy per nucleon is a maximum
products of splitting a 56Fe nucleus must have less binding energy
(reaction would require) a net input of energy

hints: Hint 1: Recall the shape of the binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number curve, and remember where $^{56}_{26}$Fe sits on that curve.
Hint 2: Compare the binding energy per nucleon of the starting Fe nucleus with that of the lighter products $^{20}_{9}$F and $^{37}_{17}$Cl - is it higher or lower?
Hint 3: Link a change in total binding energy to energy release - think about whether energy is released when binding energy increases or when it decreases.
parts.proper_answer: $^{56}$Fe has one of the highest binding energies per nucleon, near the maximum of the curve. The product nuclei F and Cl have lower binding energy per nucleon, so total binding energy decreases. This requires a net input of energy, so no overall release of energy occurs.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember where iron sits on the curve**
If you sketch binding energy per nucleon $E_b/A$ against mass number $A$, it rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks around $A = 56$ for iron, then slowly falls for heavy nuclei. Iron-56 is at the top - it is the most stable nucleus with maximum $E_b/A$.

Step 2: **Compare parent and daughters**
Here the parent is $^{56}_{26}$Fe itself. The proposed daughters $^{20}_{9}$F and $^{37}_{17}$Cl are both lighter with $A = 20$ and $A = 37$. Moving left down the curve from the peak, their binding energy per nucleon is lower than that of Fe.

Step 3: **Link binding energy to energy release**
Energy is only released in a nuclear reaction if the total binding energy increases, because the increase in binding comes from a decrease in mass via $\Delta E = \Delta m c^2$. Here total binding energy would decrease and total mass would increase, so you would have to put energy in. That is why splitting Fe-56 cannot release energy - fission only releases energy for heavy nuclei well above iron.
